operations.value:
internal/cli takes about 13 minutes to test. It is the slowest package by a wide margin — gitstore is roughly 6 minutes, perf about 3, and everything else is seconds — and the cost is no longer only patience.

## What it actually costs

It exceeds Go's default 600s timeout, so a bare 'go test ./...' reports internal/cli as FAILED rather than slow. Every newcomer and every agent hits that, and CI only passes because the workflow specifies a 45m timeout.

It also exceeds what a single foreground tool call can wait for. During the priorities work this caused a specific, repeated failure: agents would start the suite in the background, end their turn to wait for it, and never receive the result — six separate agents lost turns that way before the workflow was changed so that only the controller ran the full suite. The eventual workaround was running it in name-prefix slices, which works but means nobody runs the whole package casually.

And it discourages the run that catches the most. Three separate findings in that work were only visible in a full-package run: two configdisplay tests whose names do not match any obvious -run filter, and a core regression a targeted filter would have missed entirely.

## What to look at

Start by measuring rather than guessing. 'go test ./internal/cli -v' with timing, or -json piped through something that sorts by duration, will say whether this is a long tail of many tests or a handful of slow ones.

Strong suspicion worth checking first: most of these tests shell out to the real version control binary and build real repositories on disk. Look at how many create a repository, how many could share one, and whether t.Parallel is used at all. testrepo.New and initializedRepository are the likely hot spots.

Also worth checking:
- Whether the CLI binary is rebuilt per test or per package.
- Whether any test sleeps or waits on a deadline rather than a condition. The serve tests had one of these; there may be more.
- Whether the projection (SQLite) is rebuilt more often than it needs to be.

## What good looks like

Under the default 600s timeout would be the single biggest win, because it makes 'go test ./...' work with no flags for everyone. Under five minutes would make the full package something people run before pushing rather than something they avoid.

## Not urgent, and do not trade correctness for it

These tests are slow largely because they exercise real repositories and real command-line surfaces, which is why they catch what they catch. A faster suite that stopped touching real repositories would be a worse suite. Prefer sharing setup and running in parallel over replacing integration coverage with mocks.
